evidence.question: What error or warning lines does frontend emit around 10:59:24, and do they name a downstream callee, a timeout, or an exception type?

findings.note: The window requested ends at 10:59:29 but log coverage stops at 10:53:06. The ~6-minute silence is itself ambiguous: it may mean the frontend emitted nothing (steady-state INFO suppressed) or that log shipping lagged/dropped. Answering the 10:59:24 question requires a different source — downstream service logs, traces, or request metrics at that timestamp. Also note the restart at 10:53:05 is worth correlating with the incident start; the Consul refusal suggests Consul itself was unavailable or restarting at that moment.

found.statement: The frontend log stream for the 30-minute window contains no error or warning lines at or near 10:59:24; the only non-INFO lines in the entire window are clustered at 10:53:05, roughly six minutes before the time of interest.

The error lines present at 10:53:05 are service-discovery failures: the frontend's Consul-backed gRPC load balancer could not retrieve instances for two named services (srv-profile and srv-search), failing with a TCP connection-refused to the Consul agent endpoint on port 8500. These repeat several times.

The error type named is a connection refusal at dial time, not a timeout/deadline and not a language-level exception or panic. The named counterparty is the Consul agent (the discovery dependency), with srv-profile and srv-search appearing only as lookup targets, not as callees that returned errors.

The surrounding INFO lines show a full cold-start sequence at 10:53:05-10:53:06 (config read, Jaeger init, Consul agent init, gRPC client initialization for search, profile, recommendation, reservation, user, then HTTP serving), indicating the frontend process restarted at 10:53:05 and reached a serving state by 10:53:06.

The Consul discovery errors were transient relative to startup: they precede the successful gRPC client initialization lines and the serving confirmation in the same two-second span, and do not recur afterwards in the window.

ruled_out.why: No log lines of any level exist at or around 10:59:24 in this window; the stream's last entry is at 10:53:06. Frontend logs cannot supply a callee name for that moment.

ruled_out.why: No exception type, panic, or stack trace appears. The restart at 10:53:05 is followed by a clean init sequence and a successful serve, consistent with a normal process start rather than a code fault.

verdict.reasoning: Change history across a full 24 hours for two services contains exactly one suspicious act: the namespace-wide deny-all NetworkPolicy at 10:53:18, everything else being first-time stand-up of Services and workloads [tr_87652bf6467a][tr_0c99cf700f8c]. Frontend's log rules out the application-side stories - no deadline or context-cancellation wording, no panic or stack trace, and successful gRPC client init followed by an HTTP serving confirmation [tr_d3e4bb54f84b]; a crash or a slow dependency would have left one of those. The silent instruments are not negative evidence: the Prometheus error-ratio queries for frontend and profile failed structurally because neither emits span-derived metrics, over both incident and baseline windows [tr_2cca751ac3a4][tr_5dc2642b7db7], and the Tempo gap for frontend is uniform across the whole 30 minutes rather than onset-shaped [tr_2905d9ddfa34]. A deny-all policy named for the recommendation path is the mechanism that hangs a caller on one edge while the callee's process stays up - partition, not a wrong configuration value breaking a request. The fix is restoring the severed connectivity.
verdict.root_cause: At 10:53:18, about six minutes before the 10:59:24 alert, platform-automation created a NetworkPolicy `deny-all-recommendation` recorded as namespace-wide rather than narrowly selected [tr_87652bf6467a][tr_0c99cf700f8c]. That policy cuts L3/L4 connectivity on the recommendation path inside the namespace, so frontend's calls on that edge no longer reach a peer. The mechanism is connectivity removal, not an application regression: frontend's change history holds no image bump, no flag toggle and no dependency change, only first-time creation of its Service and workload [tr_87652bf6467a], and its log shows a clean cold start at 10:53:05-10:53:06 that resolved all backends and reached a serving state, with no panic, exception, timeout or downstream error afterwards [tr_d3e4bb54f84b]. The Consul connection-refused lines at 10:53:05 precede the policy and clear within two seconds, so they are startup race noise. Frontend alerted because it is the caller that notices; what broke is the recommendation path being severed.

alternatives.why_not: Same policy and mechanism, different victim, and the evidence barely separates them. It ranks second only because the policy is named for the recommendation path; frontend's log ends twelve seconds before the policy landed, so there is no post-policy frontend signal either way. One dispatch to recommendation could invert this.
alternatives.root_cause: The same namespace-wide deny-all policy isolates frontend itself rather than recommendation, cutting it off from all five backends.

alternatives.why_not: The wrong value is how this started, but what is happening now is severed connectivity; classifying by the upstream edit rather than the live mechanism. Reverting the policy is still the practical fix, so the two converge in action if not in class.
alternatives.root_cause: The policy's scope value is itself wrong - written namespace-wide when a narrow selector was intended - making the misconfiguration the failure.

open_questions: No dispatch reached recommendation itself; its logs would decide partition versus freeze, since a partitioned process complains it cannot reach anything and a frozen one writes nothing.

The policy's real selector is unresolved - one finding calls the selector metadata incomplete and says its practical effect is not established [tr_0c99cf700f8c], so the blast radius and the named service could both change.

Frontend wrote nothing after 10:53:06 [tr_d3e4bb54f84b] and emitted no spans all window [tr_2905d9ddfa34], so whether it was serving traffic at 10:59:24 - and why onset lagged the policy by six minutes - is unverified.

draft.title: Frontend alert with silent telemetry: a connectivity-removing policy on the recommendation path

sections.body:
The page came from frontend and nothing else. Severity was called critical, with six services in the blast radius and five edges crossed that nobody had measurement on. Take T+0 as the moment the alert fired on frontend.

The first instinct — open frontend's own dashboards and traces and watch the error curve bend — went nowhere, and that dead end shaped the rest of the investigation. Treat the next two sections as a warning about which instruments were simply not wired up here.
sections.heading: What the responder saw first

sections.body:
The error-ratio query against Prometheus for frontend returned nothing, for the incident window and for the half hour of baseline before it. This was not a flat zero line and it must never be read as one: the backend stated outright that it holds no span-derived series for frontend at all, because frontend does not emit traces that get converted into metrics. Absence here carries zero information about frontend health.

The same instrument failed the same way on profile. No request rate, no latency percentiles, no per-edge breakdown across frontend's four outbound dependencies. Retrying with different window bounds would not have helped — the reason given is structural, not a retention or scrape gap. If you are reading this months later: do not spend time re-running these templates on these services.
sections.heading: Dead end: the metrics were never there

sections.body:
Tempo held no frontend spans anywhere in the thirty-minute window — not thinned out near T+0, but uniformly absent from T-30m onward. That uniformity is itself mildly informative: it looks like a service whose telemetry never reached the backend, not a service that was healthy and then tipped over at the alert.

The consequence was that the most attractive hypothesis-splitting move — compare when each outbound span type stopped, and name the dependency that went first — was unavailable. All outbound edges were equally absent, so there was no differential timing to read. The timeline had to be rebuilt from logs and the change record instead.
sections.heading: Dead end: the traces were empty too

sections.body:
Frontend's log stream had no error or warning line anywhere near T+0. In fact the stream's last entry of any level is at roughly T-6m. Everything non-INFO in the whole window sits in a two-second cluster there.

That cluster is a cold start. Config read, tracing init, discovery agent init, gRPC client setup for search, profile, recommendation, reservation and user, then an HTTP serving confirmation — a complete startup sequence finishing within about a second. Interleaved with it are several connection-refused failures from the discovery-backed gRPC balancer when looking up two services. Those are dial-time refusals against the Consul agent, not timeouts, not deadline-exceeded, not a panic or stack trace. They precede the successful client-init lines in the same two seconds and never recur.

So: the discovery errors are startup race noise and were set aside. But the restart itself is real and had to go in the timeline — the assumption that frontend ran continuously and the trouble was purely downstream is contradicted by that cold start.
sections.heading: What the logs actually said

sections.body:
With metrics and traces unusable, the change history carried the investigation. Frontend's 24-hour change window holds exactly three entries, all from the platform-automation actor, inside a span of about fifteen seconds roughly six minutes before the alert. Two of them are the first-ever creation of frontend's Service and of its workload container — a fresh stand-up, not a modification. The third, landing a few seconds later at about T-6m, is the creation of a deny-all NetworkPolicy on the recommendation path, recorded with namespace-wide scope.

Profile's change record tells the same story from the other side: Service and workload created, then the same policy fourteen seconds afterwards, same actor. The brief gap between workload creation and the policy matters — pods were reachable for a moment before the policy applied, so "never reachable at all" is not the shape.

Several tempting explanations fall away against this record. There was no image bump or deploy: the only container event is a first creation, so there was no prior revision to regress. There was no flag toggle recorded. No dependency or library version moved. No slow drift or older change exists — the full 24-hour window is otherwise empty. And no human operator is named anywhere; all of it is one automation rollout, not two teams colliding.
sections.heading: The change record, which is where it turned

sections.body:
The reading is that connectivity on the recommendation path was removed inside the namespace about six minutes before the page, so frontend's calls on that edge stopped reaching a peer. The mechanism is connectivity removal rather than an application regression — frontend's own process started cleanly, resolved every backend, reached a serving state, and then logged nothing bad at all. Frontend alerted because it is the caller that notices the silence, not because frontend is what broke.

Confidence is medium. The fix class is reconnect: restore the path rather than roll back any application artifact.
sections.heading: Where we landed

sections.body:
Three things were never closed.

First, nobody pulled logs from recommendation itself. That is the single highest-value missing query. A process cut off from the network complains that it cannot reach anything; a process that has stopped executing writes nothing at all. Those two look identical from frontend's chair and recommendation's own stream would separate them.

Second, the policy's real selector is unresolved. One finding describes the selector metadata on the change record as incomplete or malformed and says its practical effect on pods is not established by that record alone. If the selector turns out narrower than the namespace-wide scope the record claims, both the blast radius and the named service could change.

Third, there is a six-minute gap nobody explained. Frontend wrote its last line at about T-6m and emitted no spans for the entire window, so there is no direct evidence it was serving traffic at T+0, and no account of why onset lagged the policy by six minutes rather than landing immediately. That lag is worth understanding before the conclusion above is treated as settled.
sections.heading: Open threads for whoever picks this up

proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is that the partition persists and the recommendation path stays severed until a human intervenes; mean time to repair lengthens by the escalation delay. The risk of the alternative - proposing restart_service or revert_config on frontend anyway - is larger: a restart discards the serving process and its caches and would not touch the L3/L4 policy, so the outage would continue with a fresh process and a new cold-start error burst muddying the timeline; a config_revert on a service whose config was created, not modified, has no prior state and could leave it unconfigured.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if the policy's real selector turns out not to cover the recommendation path - one finding calls the selector metadata incomplete and says its practical effect is not established [tr_0c99cf700f8c] - in which case the fault is something else and a different action might apply. It is also wrong if recommendation's own logs (never collected) show a frozen process rather than a partitioned one, which would make restart_service on recommendation defensible. Note that the confirming signal is itself weak here: frontend has no span metrics [tr_2905d9ddfa34] and wrote no logs after 10:53:06 [tr_d3e4bb54f84b], so any remediation's success would be hard to observe on the alerted service at all - a further reason to hold.
proposal.blast_radius: No one sees a change, because nothing is executed. The incident's existing blast radius is unchanged: frontend (alerted seed) and the five services reached from it - profile, recommendation, reservation, search, user. The humans who notice are the on-call responders, who now carry the fix rather than this system.
proposal.expected_effect: No action proposed, so no change in observables is predicted. The mechanism named by the verdict is a namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy `deny-all-recommendation` created at 10:53:18 by platform-automation [tr_87652bf6467a][tr_0c99cf700f8c]; the only effect that would clear it is removing or narrowing that policy (fix class `reconnect`), and `reconnect_service` is listed UNAVAILABLE - the executor performs only rollback_image, revert_config and restart_service. None of the three available actions meets its own preconditions here: rollback_image requires a prior image tag and a deploy/image change in the window, and the change history records no deploy and no image bump, only a first-ever workload creation [tr_87652bf6467a]; revert_config requires a prior configuration for the target service, and every recorded config event is a first creation (Service frontend, Service profile, the policy itself), so there is no earlier state to restore to [tr_87652bf6467a][tr_0c99cf700f8c]; restart_service requires evidence pointing at process state, and frontend's log shows a clean cold start reaching a serving state at 10:53:06 with no panic, exception or timeout afterwards [tr_d3e4bb54f84b], which points at connectivity removal, not at a wedged process. Escalate to an operator who can delete or re-scope the NetworkPolicy.
